funding_share_basis: The purse is a single cash prize to the laureate(s), currently USD 1,000,000. Applying the >50% test to the money: 100% of today's purse is supplied by Google, which has been the sole funder since the 2014 award; ACM contributes 0% of the cash. From 1966 to 2001 ACM paid the purse entirely from its own funds (USD 25,000 by the late 1990s, no named external sponsor); ACM's 2007 release states 'Intel has funded ACM's Turing Award since 2002' (Intel alone USD 100,000, 2002-2006; Intel and Google jointly USD 250,000, 2007-2013, shares undisclosed). So none of the original ACM money remains in today's purse - all of it is new corporate money - and the coding is true under either reading of the origin funder, since Google is neither ACM nor Intel. The 2025 award (announced March 2026) still carries the same Google-funded USD 1,000,000.
money_note: Current purse USD 1,000,000, paid entirely by Google since the 2014 award (announced November 2014, quadrupling the USD 250,000 Intel-plus-Google purse of 2007-2013); still Google-funded for the 2025 award announced March 2026.
evidence_quote: "The ACM A.M. Turing Award carries a $1 million prize, with financial support provided by Google, Inc."; "Intel has funded ACM's Turing Award since 2002." (ACM, 2007)
judgment_reason: Origin funding is inferred rather than documented in a 1966 source: ACM states corporate funding started with Intel in 2002 and the pre-2002 USD 25,000 purse carried no named sponsor, so ACM's own funds is the residual coding; a coder treating Intel's 2002 takeover as a refounding would code the origin funder as Intel (Corporate, United States). The funder_changed=true coding is unaffected by that choice, since Google funds 100% of today's purse either way.
